analysis.one_liner: Requires federal approval of bonus plans at firms that received bailout aid.
analysis.headline: The bill to require advance federal approval of employee bonuses at institutions receiving TARP or Federal Reserve aid was never acted on after its referral to the House Financial Services Committee and died when the 111th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required banks and other financial firms that received taxpayer bailout money through the Troubled Asset Relief Program (TARP) or emergency Federal Reserve lending to get their employee bonus plans approved by the Treasury Secretary before paying any bonuses. It was aimed at stopping executives at rescued firms from paying themselves large bonuses while the public was covering their losses. The bill was introduced in March 2009 and referred to the House Financial Services Committee, which never took it up.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers and the public, who bore the cost of the 2008 financial bailouts and would have gained a check on bonus payments at rescued firms; rank-and-file employees of rescued firms, whose bonus plans would also have needed approval, limiting payouts skewed toward executives.

how_it_helps.text: It would have required the Treasury Secretary to approve any employee bonus payment plan at institutions receiving TARP assistance before bonuses could be paid [S2][S3].
It would have imposed the same requirement on firms receiving emergency Federal Reserve lending under section 13 of the Federal Reserve Act, closing a route around TARP rules [S3].
It defined bonus payments to include, at minimum, retention compensation and incentive compensation, the categories commonly used to pay large sums to executives [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Executives and highly paid employees of bailed-out financial institutions, who would have lost unilateral control over bonus payouts at firms kept afloat with public money, and the firms themselves, which would have faced federal oversight of their compensation practices.

drawbacks.text: The bill gave Treasury and the Federal Reserve wide discretion: Treasury would define what counts as a bonus payment, and no standards were set for what plans must be approved or denied, which could have produced arbitrary or politicized decisions [S3].

Critics of executive pay restrictions argue that capping or delaying bonuses can push talented staff out of struggling firms or drive compensation into harder-to-trace forms, weakening firms the public was trying to stabilize; this bill's approval requirement would have applied to all employee bonuses, not only executive ones.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public benefit was a direct check on bonuses at firms rescued with taxpayer money, addressing one of the most publicized outrages of the 2008 crisis; the cost fell on compensation practices at a small set of rescued institutions. The bill's reliance on unguided Treasury discretion was a real design weakness, but it applied only to institutions receiving new federal assistance, a narrow and defensible scope.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Financial Services Committee after its referral and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Christopher Murphy introduced the bill on March 19, 2009 [S1][S2].
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services, and no further action was ever recorded [S5].
No member joined as a cosponsor during the entire Congress [S4].
The bill never advanced past committee, and the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011, killing it [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Executives and bonus recipients at financial institutions receiving federal bailout assistance kept the freedom to set and pay bonuses without advance federal approval; nothing in the bill ever took effect.

for.name: Rep. Christopher Murphy
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill requiring advance federal approval of bonus plans at TARP and Federal Reserve-assisted institutions

against.name: House Committee on Financial Services
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over TARP and financial regulation
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill

against.name: Financial services industry
against.role: Banks and financial firms receiving federal assistance
against.what_they_did: Had a direct interest in blocking federal approval of compensation at rescued firms; no lobbying activity is documented in the record for this bill

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and no other member signed on, so the partisan split on the bill cannot be measured; the sponsor was a Democrat.

industries.industry: Financial institutions receiving federal bailout aid
industries.note: The bill would have subjected their bonus plans to advance approval by Treasury or the Fed, limiting compensation payouts at firms kept afloat with public money. Because it applied only to firms receiving new federal assistance, the burden fell on the rescued institutions rather than the industry at large.

industries.industry: Wall Street compensation practices (executives and bonus recipients)
industries.note: Executives and highly paid employees at rescued firms would have lost control over the timing and structure of retention and incentive pay, the categories the bill explicitly targeted.
